references.context: Set theory: bijective mapping f:X→Y, a function that is both injective and surjective onto the specified codomain Y; equivalently a function admitting a two-sided inverse Y→X. In structured settings this refers only to the underlying-set map, not to automatic continuity, R-linearity, group structure, or naturality.
references.matching_note: This is bijectivity of the underlying function; the source retains the independent topological inverse-continuity, graph-edge equivalence, Hom comparison naturality or ordinal representative hypotheses. The two defining conditions injective and surjective are not confused with an isomorphism of structured objects.

references.disposition: Continuity of the inverse Y→X is an essential defining condition of a homeomorphism, not a separate object needing another name. Bijectivity and general topological continuity are already independently referenced. Existence of the set-theoretic inverse follows from bijectivity, but inverse-continuity does not; it must remain explicitly required.
The separate inverse-continuity requirement is essential.

references.disposition: Under the explicit bijection hypothesis, the equivalence for every U⊆X between U open in X and f[U] open in Y is exactly this source's defining characterization of homeomorphism; underlying continuity and direct image have existing targets. It is stronger than only requiring the map be open, and must hold for ALL subsets, not merely a selected U.
The iff criterion encodes continuity of map and inverse, not merely preservation of openness in one direction.

The existing filtration, real random-variable and probability-measurability concepts supply the mathematical prerequisites, with F_n replacing the ambient F in the preimage test; it is not a separately missing notion of adapted process.
